The drug Steve has taken is most likely to be MDMA (M dance about).  This is featured in the 'Year 1 Psych of Health/Anxiety and Psychosis' lecture.  MDMA causes a surge in serotonin, dopamine and norepinephrine.  It has an initial phase of euphoria, increased energy and decreased inhibition.  Physiological effects include increased heart rate and temperature, dilated pupils and dehydration (hence why Steve feels like he needs to drink water).  It is anti-psychotic in nature in the short term (hence Steve not experiencing any delusions or hallucinations) but it is important to note that it is not a long term solution and can actually lead to psychosis after several hours (hence Steve feeling irritable and anxious as the drug wears off).  Other effects include closed M3 receptors (hence why Steve is unable to urinate - bladder flap paralysis).  The other drugs are not likely to cause these symptoms.  Amphetamines and cocaine are similar to MDMA in that they increase the levels of dopamine, norepinephrine and serotonin but they have a more severe sympathetic nervous system response (more so than MDMA).  Cannabis causes an increase in the levels of dopamine in the reward pathway (nucleus accumbens and ventral tegmental area) and the release of endocannabinoids.  LSD is a serotonergic psychedelic and it binds to 5-HT2A receptors.

Hyperthyroidism is caused by an excess of thyroid hormones.  Carbimazole works by inhibiting iodine uptake in the thyroid gland, preventing the formation of thyroid hormones.  Iodine is essential for the synthesis of T3 and T4.  Iodine is trapped in the thyroid gland via the sodium-iodide symporter, which couples the inward movement of iodine with the inward movement of sodium.  The enzyme thyroglobulin, produced by follicular cells, then oxidises the trapped iodide to form hypoiodous acid (HOI), which reacts with thyroglobulin to form monoiodothyroglobulin (MIT) and diiodothyroglobulin (DIT).  Thyroid hormones are then released as free T4 and thyroxine-bound T3 from thyroglobulin.  Levothyroxine is synthetic T4 and may be given to treat hypothyroidism.  Triodothyronine (T3) is the biologically active form of the thyroid hormone.  Insulin is used to treat diabetes.  Hydrocortisone is used to treat adrenal insufficiency.

The answer is the foramen ovale. This is part of a whole that includes the ductus arteriosus and the fossa ovalis.  The foramen ovale is an opening between the left and right atria that allows blood to move from the right to the left atria to bypass the just formed tricuspid and semilunar valves and the intra-atrial septum. It is open during foetal circulation to allow the oxygenated blood from the placenta to bypass the right ventricle and pulmonary circulation. After birth when the baby takes its first breath, the pressure in the left atria increases and the right decreases, meaning that the foramen ovale is closed.  The septum primum and septum secundum meet to form the fossa ovalis. The remnant of the foramen ovale that is left after the closure of the foramen ovale. The ductus arteriosus is a vessel that allows blood to move from the pulmonary artery to the aorta, bypassing the right ventricle and ascending aorta. It closes a few hours after birth and is replaced by the ligamentum arteriosum.  The left umbilical vein does allow blood to bypass the foetal liver and is replaced by the ligamentum teres.

Calsequestrin is the correct answer. It is found in the ryanodine receptor and keeps Ca2+ locked in the SR of the cell. Increased Ca2+ in the cell (ie. via L-type Ca2+ channels during a cardiac action potential) removes this effect and causes calcium-induced-calcium release.  Calbindin is a Ca2+ binding protein that is found in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (ie. in VSMC). It increases the capacity of the SR to store Ca2+. Calmodulin is a Ca2+ binding protein that regulates various enzymes (ie. myosin light chain kinase) when it binds Ca2+. Phospholamban inhibits SERCA (smooth endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase) and prevents Ca2+ being stored in the SR. However, when VSMC are stimulated by agonist (ie. adrenaline), this causes a phosphorylation of phospholamban which removes this inhibition and causes an increase in Ca2+ storage in the SR. SERCA is a Ca2+ ATPase that pumps Ca2+ into the SR.
